claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain and toughness in fusion-relevant tungsten-based materials or high-performance steels are dominantly governed by competition between dynamic dislocation recovery and grain-boundary-mediated processes.
Dynamic dislocation recovery in these materials occurs through dislocation climb and cross-slip.
The relevant grain-boundary-mediated processes are grain-boundary sliding and decohesion.
Increasing radiation-induced defect density shifts the balance between dynamic recovery and grain-boundary-mediated processes.
Controlled pre-irradiation or ion-beam treatment can be used to increase radiation-induced defect density.
Radiation-induced defects provide additional sites for dislocation climb.
Radiation-induced defects provide additional sites for dislocation cross-slip.
The additional climb and cross-slip sites enhance dynamic dislocation recovery.
Radiation-induced defects may concentrate stress at grain boundaries.
Defect-induced grain-boundary stress concentration promotes grain-boundary sliding and decohesion.
Macroscopic plastic strain and toughness reflect the relative dominance of dynamic recovery and grain-boundary degradation.
Irradiated samples should exhibit a measurable change in high-temperature plastic strain or toughness relative to a low-defect baseline.
When increased defect density favors dynamic recovery, plastic strain and ductility should increase.
When increased defect density favors dynamic recovery, toughness may increase.
When grain-boundary decohesion becomes dominant at higher defect densities, toughness should decrease.
High-temperature mechanical response is sensitively dependent on radiation-induced defect density within the tested regime.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply from 600°C to 1200°C under controlled transient thermal or mechanical loading.
Much lower temperatures or extreme irradiation levels may activate additional mechanisms outside the proposed regime.
